Expert Quote: "Education and awareness are significant pieces of the puzzle," — Chris Birk, Vice President of Mortgage Insight, Veterans United Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Mortgage lenders could have made approximately 83,100 mortgages, representing $41 billion in volume in 2025 through the Veterans Affairs mortgage guarantee program, an analysis from Veterans United Home Loans found. This was an increase from a $37.9 billion gap one year prior. The share of VA loans originated remains lower than the number of eligible borrowers in dozens of housing markets, the report claimed. Why aren't eligible borrowers seeking a VA mortgage "Education and awareness are significant pieces of the puzzle," said Chris Birk, vice president of mortgage insight at Veterans United. "Some Veterans may not fully understand the benefits they've earned, while others may be working with real estate agents who aren't as familiar with VA financing." Birk also pointed to the persistent misconceptions about VA loans which can influence how borrowers, agents and sellers approach these transactions which seek this form of financing. Past surveys, including one from Navy Federal Credit Union , showed many veterans had erroneous ideas about the VA program, including not being aware it offers 100% loan-to-value ratio mortgages. A NewDay USA survey from this past April of current or past servicemembers and reservists found that about 13% said they were extremely well educated, with 20% very well educated, about their mortgage benefit. The leading response was somewhat at 35%, followed by hardly at 19% and not well educated at all by 13%. What is the role of housing affordability in the VA use gap Part of the problem might be general affordability. Just under 8% of homes for sale as of Oct. 23 were within the reach of a veteran who earns his or her local median income, with a 100% LTV, a study from Movoto by Lower stated. The study used the then-current 7.32% average rate for a VA mortgage at 28% of median income for veterans who live in a particular metro area. Movoto found 86,277 of over 1.11 million homes listed for sale in 196 metro areas were affordable to this group; the data did not include calculations for taxes and insurance, which also impacts monthly mortgage payments. Nationwide, veterans represent 6.2% of the adult population. The largest numbers are in New York City, Washington and Dallas-Fort Worth. But the highest shares for where veterans live are in Jacksonville, North Carolina, 21.8%; Killeen-Temple, Texas, 19.2%; and Fayetteville, North Carolina, 18%. All three are where large military installations are located, Movoto said. Where are the opportunities to market VA mortgages In the Veterans United study, New York is also the largest metro for untapped VA borrowers. The study looked at estimates of potential lender opportunity for these loans, so it did not take into account veterans who used another mortgage product to purchase a home. "The geographic differences are telling," Birk said. Markets with a strong military presence, those close to bases for example, tend to have higher VA loan utilization. But in some metros with larger veteran populations, they might not have as much knowledge about the program. "That suggests awareness could be playing an important role," Birk said. It's not necessarily that Veterans are being denied access to the benefit, but many may not be getting the information or guidance they need to fully explore it. "That's something the entire industry can work to improve," he said. It estimated how many VA mortgages could be made in a metro area if its usage reached the national benchmark. In the New York metro area, it said an additional 3,597 loans could be made. This was followed by Philadelphia and nearby cities at 2,678 and Chicago at 2,410. Los Angeles was fourth at 2,305. Meanwhile, Movoto said Macon, Georgia is the market where veterans can afford the largest share of homes for sale, at 35.6%. Youngtown, Ohio was next at 34.9%, followed by Pittsburgh at 30.9%. How many VA mortgage apps were received this week The Mortgage Bankers Association's Weekly Application Survey put the VA share of total applications for the period ended Nov. 6 at 12.4%, up from 11.2% the week prior. In comparison, the share of Federal Housing Administration mortgages fell to 15.5% from 16%. "Applications for conventional, VA and FHA purchase applications saw gains over the week, with particularly strong growth for FHA and VA loans," said Joel Kan, the group's deputy chief economist, in a press release. "Refinance applications also saw a relatively strong week, with a big rebound in VA refinance applications over the past two weeks." The MBA does not have data on how many of those refis were the VA Interest Rate Reduction Refinance Loan, versus mortgages coming from another product like conventional or FHA. How many borrowers locked a VA mortgage in October? The Optimal Blue Market Advantage report for October found the 30-year VA mortgage averaged 6.76% compared with 7.15% for conforming and 7% for FHA. items.title: Hurricane Season Is Over Early, but El Niño Is Not Done With Us Yet
items.description: In a typical year, the Atlantic hurricane season runs from June to the end of November. But 2026 has been anything but a typical year. In fact, the meteorologists at AccuWeather have announced that tropical activity for the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season is over, three weeks before the official end of the season on Nov. 30. The reason? "El Niño has played a significant role in limiting tropical activity across the Atlantic," said AccuWeather lead hurricane expert Alex DaSilva . "While tropical storms can still develop this late in the season, the weather patterns we're seeing give us confidence that the United States will avoid additional direct tropical impacts this year. It's an unusually quiet conclusion to a season that defied expectations and broke a 121-year-old hurricane record.” But while the hurricane season might be bowing out early, the country still needs to prepare itself for the coming winter months in a big way. A quiet season AccuWeather originally forecasted 11 to 16 named storms for the season last spring, but once El Niño arrived and strengthened much earlier in the year than usual, the forecast dropped to eight to 11 named storms and three to four hurricanes. To date, only 10 named storms came to fruition, the fewest since 2014, when there were only eight storms. Only one reached hurricane status, with Hurricane Isaias making a destructive Category 2 landfall on the Florida Panhandle in October. It was the first time since 1925 that there was only one hurricane in the entire season. That’s not to say that the season wasn’t destructive. The first storm of the season, Tropical Storm Arthur , dumped more than 20 inches of rain in some spots across the Gulf in June and caused an estimated $4 billion to $6 billion in total damage and economic loss, according to a preliminary estimate from experts at AccuWeather . Loading... Loading... Hurricanes out, but wet weather remains While the hurricane season is over, homeowners across the country still have to continue with a deluge of wet weather on the way. Again, all thanks to the Super El Niño still churning away. Notably, the El Niño could influence winter weather across the United States, bringing warmer-than-average temperatures to Northern states and wetter-than-average conditions to the South and East Coast, according to NOAA’s U.S. Winter Outlook . Wetter-than-average conditions are most likely across the southern tier, from the Southwest to the Southeast, and along the East Coast. But if the temperatures stay up, the likelihood of snow is slim. But even without the snow , the storms could be significant for this area this year. “As we know from decades of observations, a very strong El Nino will likely bring a southward and eastward shift to the jet stream for the contiguous U.S., which tilts the odds toward stormier weather across the South,” said Ken Graham , director of NOAA’s National Weather Service. “While higher chances of rain and snow may bring relief to drought-afflicted areas, too much precipitation on dry soil can fuel destructive flash floods and mudslides. Now is the time for communities and individuals to plan ahead for the upcoming winter.” Meanwhile, more snow than average is favored across parts of the Intermountain West, the Plains, and the Appalachians this winter because of El Niño's active storm track, according to The Wall Street Journal . In fact, most models that were reviewed showed above-average snowfall across the Plains, from South Dakota to northern Texas , and a swath of the central and southern Appalachians. items.title: This New Water Heater Gadget Could Turn Your Hot Showers Into Bitcoin. But Is It Worth It?
items.description: Your water heater already uses electricity to keep the showers hot and dishes clean. But what if it could also earn you a little money at the same time? That's the idea behind Bitwater , an unusual new home appliance from technology company Heatbit that combines an electric water heater's heating element with a bitcoin mining computer. Rather than purchasing an entirely new water heater, homeowners can install the device inside an existing electric tank, replacing a conventional heating element with one powered by computer chips that generate heat while mining cryptocurrency . "We were actually looking for areas where electricity is turned into heat, where it's not seasonal," Alex Busarov , Heatbit's founder, told Realtor.com® in a phone interview. The company had already developed bitcoin-mining space heaters, he explained, but household water heating offered an opportunity to put the technology to work year-round. It's an eye-catching proposition at a time when homeowners are looking for ways to offset utility bills. But can mining bitcoin really make heating water more affordable? How does a bitcoin-mining water heater work? At first glance, Bitwater resembles an oversized heating element, the metal component inside an electric water heater that warms the water. But instead of a traditional electrical resistance wire, it contains specialized computer chips that perform the calculations involved in bitcoin mining . But instead of a traditional electrical resistance wire, it contains specialized computer chips that perform the calculations involved in bitcoin mining . Those chips produce heat as they work. Bitwater transfers that heat into the surrounding water, cooling the computer hardware while heating the tank. Loading... A look inside the Heatbit unit HEATBIT Unlike space heating, which is largely unnecessary during the warmer months, households need hot water throughout the year. That makes a water heater a potentially more practical home for computing equipment that generates heat. The device replaces only the lower heating element in a conventional electric water heater . The upper element remains in place to provide additional heating when demand increases. According to Busarov, Bitwater typically operates at approximately 400 to 600 watts, heating water more gradually than a conventional element that might draw several thousand watts for a shorter period. Busarov said the device automatically stops mining when the water reaches its target temperature. He estimated that the mining hardware operates approximately 80% of the time, although actual utilization would depend on household demand for hot water. Can it actually save—or make—you money? Bitwater can reportedly generate up to 34 terahashes per second, a measure of the computing power used to mine bitcoin, which Busarov estimated could translate to roughly $30 per month in cryptocurrency under current mining conditions. That would represent approximately $360 annually, although actual earnings depend on bitcoin prices, mining difficulty, operating time, and other factors. At that rate, a roughly $900 device would require about 2.5 years to recover its purchase price, even before accounting for installation costs, mining fees, maintenance, or changes in cryptocurrency earnings. There is an important distinction, however, between generating bitcoin revenue and saving energy. Bitwater doesn't eliminate the electricity needed to heat water. Instead, the company argues that the electricity can perform two useful jobs: powering a computer and producing household hot water. In principle, that gives the homeowner some cryptocurrency in exchange for electricity that would otherwise have gone toward conventional resistance heating. Busarov says the mining operation shuts down when the tank reaches its desired temperature, so the device isn't intended to consume additional electricity solely to mine bitcoin. It prioritizes heating water, with cryptocurrency mining as a secondary function. At an illustrative electricity rate of 18 cents per kilowatt-hour, operating a 600-watt device continuously would consume about $78 in electricity each month. Bitwater is not designed to operate continuously, however, and that electricity would not necessarily represent an additional expense if the heat replaces what a conventional electric heating element would otherwise produce. Heatbit's projected earnings are therefore not the same as guaranteed savings on a utility bill. The calculation depends on how much the device operates and how much cryptocurrency it actually generates. What about installation and safety? Loading... DIY installation kit for Heatbit HEATBIT Heatbit designed Bitwater as a retrofit for conventional electric tank water heaters rather than a complete replacement system. The device is intended to fit compatible residential tanks equipped with standard screw-in heating elements. Busarov said installation is designed to be comparable to replacing an ordinary water heater element. "We really built it for DIY installation," he said. That doesn't necessarily mean every homeowner should attempt it. Working on a water heater involves electricity, pressurized water, and potential flooding hazards. Homeowners unfamiliar with those systems should use a qualified professional and check local code requirements. Heatbit promotes several safety and maintenance features, including leak protection, overheating safeguards, and programmed high-temperature cycles intended to limit the growth of Legionella bacteria. Busarov said protecting against leaks was a significant part of developing the physical product. He also described a system that can periodically raise water temperatures to combat bacterial growth without maintaining those higher temperatures continuously. items.title: Newrez partners with Upgrade to add personal loans for servicing customers
items.description: Multichannel lender Newrez partnered with financial technology firm Upgrade to offer unsecured personal loans to eligible mortgage servicing customers, giving homeowners another option to access cash without tapping home equity or refinancing. The loans, originated and serviced by Upgrade and issued by its partner Cross River Bank , do not change the existing Newrez mortgage. Newrez funded $12.9 billion in mortgages in the third quarter and reached $878.9 billion in unpaid principal balance across its mortgage servicing rights (MSR) portfolio at the end of September. According to the company, the loans can be funded in as little as one business day for qualified borrowers, have no prepayment fees and allow customers to see prequalified offers through a soft credit inquiry. Newrez framed the launch as an extension of its relationships with homeowners beyond the mortgage, with loans designed for uses such as debt consolidation , home improvements and unexpected expenses. “Our relationship with homeowners doesn't begin and end with a mortgage,” Leslie Gillin , Newrez's chief commercial officer, said in a statement. “Homeowners' financial needs often extend beyond their monthly mortgage payment , and we're proud to broaden the ways we can support them, including helping identify opportunities for savings as they navigate important financial decisions.” The launch comes as many homeowners are struggling with revolving debt. In a June 2026 survey conducted by Morning Consult on behalf of Newrez, 51% of homeowners reported carrying credit card balances , with 59% saying the debt is negatively affecting their finances. The online survey of 2,203 U.S. adults was conducted in June 2026. “The findings show that many homeowners are looking for ways to improve their financial position but may not know where to start,” Gillin said. “By combining education with access to responsible financing options, we can help customers make informed decisions that support their long-term financial goals.” This article was generated using HousingWire Automation and reviewed by a HousingWire editor before publication. items.title: UWM rolls out 40 bps year-end pricing bonus, expands Bilt partnership
items.description: United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM) this week announced the launch of a year-end pricing incentive for broker loans and an expansion of its partnership with Bilt . Effective immediately through Dec. 31, brokers who use UWM’s Underwriting+ , TRAC+ or virtual closing tools will receive 40 basis points on all agency and nonagency products when the borrower has a credit score of at least 700, UWM said. The incentive is intended to give brokers more pricing flexibility in the final weeks of 2026 while encouraging use of the lender’s underwriting and closing technology. Year-end pricing specials are common in the wholesale channel as lenders seek to pull volume into the current year, clean up pipelines and help partners hit production goals. UWM – which was more aggressive on pricing in the past but is seeking to deleverage its balance sheet amid a deal with Oaktree Capital Management and the Ishbia family – saw its gain-on-sale margins decline to 124 basis points in the third quarter, down from 133 basis points in the second quarter. UWM chairman, CEO and president Mat Ishbia told analysts he expects margins to be steady, adding that “people don’t use UWM because we’re the lowest rates” and arguing that competitors offering lower rates are not good partners. Separately, UWM said it's expanding its partnership with Bilt, a neighborhood commerce and rewards platform, to bring Bilt Neighborhood OS into its servicing ecosystem. Bilt Neighborhood OS is designed to help businesses reach customers and build loyalty through neighborhood-level experiences. Through UWM, it links mortgage servicing with homeownership tasks and local commerce, while keeping independent brokers visible to borrowers after closing. “The broker who helps you buy your home should be your first call when you’re ready to take the next step, whether that’s refinancing, accessing equity or buying again,” Ishbia said in a statement. “With Bilt Neighborhood OS, we’re making the servicing experience more valuable to homeowners and creating more reasons for them to stay connected to their broker between those major decisions.” UWM already services hundreds of thousands of loans through Bilt, giving these homeowners a single place to manage their mortgage and access rewards. With Neighborhood OS added, UWM said the experience will extend into more day-to-day homeownership activities, from finding a local contractor to exploring neighborhood offers, or reconnecting with a broker about a home equity or refinance opportunity. Bilt said it has delivered more than $1 billion in value to its 8 million members, who redeem rewards toward travel, housing payments, student loans , dining and other categories. The company also says it powers one in four U.S. rental homes , primarily through the Bilt Alliance of large owners and operators. items.description: The world’s largest industrial developer is bringing a California-sized warehouse to a city roughly 50 miles south of Downtown Atlanta. Courtesy of Prologis Prologis 75 Commerce Park in Jackson, Georgia Prologis broke ground on a 1.29M SF speculative distribution facility at its Prologis 75 Commerce Center in Jackson, Georgia, the company announced this week. “With its scale and market-leading specs, this project will help meet demand from businesses for modern, well-located facilities while also providing the flexibility, capacity and access needed to grow their operations,” Prologis Vice President Grant Benson said in a press release. Prologis operates more than 20M SF of distribution space in Georgia. Its latest project comes amid a surge in leasing activity in the Metro Atlanta industrial market. Net absorption reached 6.7M SF in the third quarter — more than double the second quarter — with leasing activity reaching an all-time high of 22.2M SF, according to a CBRE report . CBRE said leasing activity is being driven by big-box tenants in third-party logistics, automotive supply chain and infrastructure spaces. Developers have responded to the activity by kicking off 17 new projects totaling 4.2M SF in the third quarter, according to CBRE. Prologis’ newest facility will be among the few warehouses in Georgia with roofs that span up to 42 feet high, about 10 feet taller than the typical ceiling height. “Clear height is becoming an issue, not really for manufacturers, but for some users in California. The new norm for buildings in California is 42, 46 clear,” McDonald Development President Austin McDonald said during Bisnow ’s Southeast Industrial Summit earlier this month . “As those things tend to happen, I think that’ll come across the country over the next 12, 24 months.” DEVELOPMENT Downtown Atlanta hospital system Grady Health is developing a nearly 6K SF urgent care clinic in the city’s Cabbage Town neighborhood. Grady submitted an application earlier this month with the city of Atlanta to break ground on the facility at the corner of Memorial Drive and Estoria Street. The single-story project will include 44 parking spaces, two intake rooms, six exam rooms, a treatment room, three offices and an X-ray room, according to the application. The cost is $6M. *** Beverly Hills-based Kennedy Wilson broke ground on Caldwell, a 382-unit apartment complex in Sandy Springs on the site of a former UPS office at 35 Glenlake Parkway . Kennedy Wilson bought the 7-acre site and its 133K SF office building from UPS in December for $16.5M, Bisnow previously reported . The project is part of Kennedy Wilson’s first joint venture with Shimizu Corp., a development financed with a $90M construction loan from Santander Bank, according to a press release. Amenities will include a 2K SF fitness center, a wellness suite with infrared sauna and cold plunge, a resort-style pool, an outdoor beer and wine garden and grilling stations. SALES Ares Management sold 570 Horizon Drive Building 200, a 264,500 SF distribution center in Suwanee, for $41M to a New York-based LLC called KBH 85HarborRoad, according to sales tax documents filed with the Georgia Superior Court Clerks' Cooperative Authority database. The address of the LLC is tied to the nonprofit James and Bokhwa Kim Foundation Inc., according to the online foundation directory Instrumentl . According to Gwinnett County property records , it last sold in 2018 to “multiple owners” for $86M and was valued by the county at $15.4M this year. *** An LLC tied to Malibu-based American Commercial Equities purchased the Everhill Kennesaw apartments at 3238 Hidden Forest Court for $60.1M from an LLC tied to Atlanta-based Terwilliger Pappas, according to sales tax documents filed with the Georgia Superior Court Clerks' Cooperative Authority database. PERSONNEL Perkins&Will promoted Katy Daugharty to regional K-12 education practice leader for the Southeast, succeeding Barbara Crum, who is set to retire this year after three decades in the business, the company announced in a press release. Daugharty will lead the K-12 division of the architectural firm for its territories in Georgia, Alabama, the Carolinas and Florida. She joined the firm in 2024 and has more than 20 years of industry experience. *** Courtesy of Prologis Partners Finance Managing Director Lisel Morris Lisel Morris, co-founder of hotel development and advisory firm Meter Haus, has joined Partners Finance as managing director for the Southeast. She will be tasked with raising capital and nurturing investor relationships with private clients and family offices. Partners Finance is the financing division of Partners Real Estate. Morris has 15 years of experience and previously served as director of investor relations for The Allen Morris Co. in Miami, where she helped originate $50M in equity from family offices and high net worth investors and secure $160M in institutional debt. Partners Real Estate also hired Alex Battle as vice president on the office leasing team. Battle was previously director of development for the True North 400 Community Improvement District. Battle will focus on office leasing in the North Fulton County submarket starting Jan. 4. LEASES Posh modern furniture retailer Article is opening a new store in Atlanta. The firm is leasing 12K SF at Westside Provisions District, with the store slated to open in the third quarter of 2027. Article opened its first store in 2024 and plans to roll out five other stores in the coming year, including a location in Austin, according to a press release. items.title: Apartment Loans Fuel A Booming CRE CLO Market Not Seen Since 2021
items.description: Demand for apartment bridge loans is pushing CRE collateralized loan obligation issuance to heights not seen since 2021. Investors bought up $40.2B worth of the debt in the first 10 months of the year, up 66% from last year by dollar volume, according to data from Trepp provided to Bisnow . But volatile debt markets have left some issuers waiting on the sidelines for now, which is likely to weigh on fourth-quarter issuance. “I think there's a number of issuers who could have come to market in Q4 but instead are acting a little slower and looking to bring their deals to market in January,” said David Henschke, managing director and head of capital markets at Benefit Street Partners , an alternative credit asset manager and CRE CLO issuer. Bisnow/created with Google Gemini Henschke forecasts a modest level of new CRE CLO issuance through the end of the year, and he suspects the total will fall short of the $45.4B record from 2021. Investors are struggling to divine the direction of interest rates and are waiting to deploy capital until after the Federal Reserve votes at its meeting in December, he said. “We'll see what the Fed does there, and then you'll have some of that uncertainty kind of behind you,” he said. It’s that same uncertainty that is driving up CRE CLO issuance in the first place. Underlying loans bundled into CRE CLOs are typically bridge or transitional debt with two- or three-year terms. The majority of CRE CLOs today are made up of loans being used to refinance existing mortgages, but the capital is also used by developers as a transitional loan for a newly completed project on its way to full occupancy and by buyers looking for short-term acquisition financing before securing a longer-dated mortgage. “What the CRE CLO market is designed to do is be a bridge facility, and that’s what it’s doing,” said Andy Boettcher, who leads research at Trepp. “It’s bridging new product that hit during a supply wave that didn’t hit its lease-up target, and it just needs time.” The CRE CLO market was built for these transitional market phases, where there’s a sudden glut of new development as the U.S. saw during the pandemic era, he said. The loans are typically floating-rate debt, which leads to higher borrowing costs when interest rates climb, and the debt has been the fastest-growing segment of the nonagency CMBS market this year, according to Morgan Stanley . https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/30869666/visualisation.json?ref=embed-script Multifamily loans make up nearly three-quarters of all CRE CLO debt issued this year through October, and 57% of assets underwritten for CRE CLOs were built within the last five years, according to Trepp. The makeup is a shift away from the retail and office assets that were being pledged as collateral in the recent past, Morgan Stanley analysts wrote in a September research note. Office exposure made up as much as a quarter of CRE CLO collateral prior to 2020 but shrank to just 2% of issuance through this August, according to the investment bank. Some owners with maturing debt are looking at a landscape where the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield climbed above 5% before retreating and are opting to take the shorter-term CRE CLO debt as a way to effectively bet on lower debt costs within a few years. “The cost of equity, getting new equity in from somewhere else on one of these deals that has to be refinanced, is more expensive than three years of building the lease roll, stabilizing the occupancy, stabilizing the rent roll, and saying, ‘I now have a bigger value than I had going in,’” Boettcher said. But there are signs that the marketplace is itself being strained by the elevated rate environment. The CRE CLO distress rate jumped from 19% in July to 28% in August, the sharpest one-month move of any deal type this year, according to Cred iQ . Single-asset, single-borrower CMBS loans, by contrast, held flat near 22%. While climbing, the CRE CLO distress rate is concentrated in a handful of large deals, not widely dispersed. Five deals account for 38% of all of the CRE CLO special servicing balance. The distress traces to loans originated in 2021 and 2022 that now account for $3B worth of CRE CLO loans in special servicing, according to Cred iQ. Investors have shaken off the rising delinquency rates because they're concentrated in a handful of loans and because investment-grade bondholders in the segment have rarely seen real losses, Henschke said. The structure typically leaves sponsors holding the first-loss position, aligning issuers with investors, making it the most conservative structure in the CMBS market, he said. Owners opting for the shorter-term debt that comes with a CRE CLO are hoping that the interest rate environment will look better when the debt comes due in a few years. Many of the assets could refinance today with a traditional mortgage, but owners are instead taking a higher interest bill today for the prospect of greater savings in the years ahead. “You have assets that probably could go fixed-rate in today's market; they're not really bridging anything to change at the property. It's really a bridge for potentially market conditions to change,” Henschke said. items.title: Skydance Eyes Real Estate Cuts, Consolidation In $6B Cost-Saving Push
items.description: James Gunn’s exit might not be the only shake-up happening at Skydance . Google Maps 1515 Broadway in New York, home to Skydance headquarters The David Ellison -led media empire Skydance, formed from the merger of Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount , is eyeing real estate cuts as it looks to move employees out of rented offices and into company-owned properties in Los Angeles, New York, Atlanta and London, CoStar News reported . The potential moves are part of an effort to save billions of dollars in annual spending. Skydance co-CEO Ynon Kreiz said on a Monday earnings call that the company hopes to achieve at least $2.2B in savings by reducing real estate and facility overhead at Warner Bros. and Paramount. “There's also a very meaningful opportunity to rationalize our office footprint,” Kreiz said. “This includes consolidating our real estate across major markets." He said Skydance has five sites in New York, seven in Los Angeles, and multiple sites in Atlanta and London. Skydance, which completed its $111B merger last month, controls about 13M SF across 120 properties on top of “millions of square feet” leased from third-party landlords, according to CoStar. In New York, Paramount has a lease for 1.6M SF at One Astor Place at 1515 Broadway through 2031 and has another 185K SF at 555 W. 57th St. through 2029. Paramount also has 797K SF in Columbia Square in Los Angeles' Hollywood through 2028 and offices in Santa Monica , California, through 2034, CoStar reported. Third-party landlords with exposure to Skydance units include Kilroy Realty , Worthe Real Estate Group and Stockbridge , CoStar found. Earlier this week, Skydance announced that it was replacing DC Studios co-CEOs James Gunn and Peter Safran with former Marvel producer Jeremy Latcham, The Hollywood Reporter reported . Ellison also outlined other cost-cutting measures, including bundling HBO Max and Paramount+ streaming services together next year, in an effort to eliminate $6B in expenses in three years as it wrangles with $80B in debt. Skydance in its merged form spent about $8B in corporate overhead, including real estate, this year, according to the LA Times . items.title: Lender Takes Control Of Vacant Somerville Lab Building Following Failed Sale
items.description: The lender on a completely vacant life sciences building that delivered two years ago has taken ownership of it and is pursuing a sale. Google Maps 808 Windsor St. in Somerville The lab building at 808 Windsor St. in Somerville was transferred to lender Bank OZK through a deed-in-lieu-of-foreclosure on Sept. 29, according to deed records. The 370K SF property was previously owned by a joint venture between Leggat McCall Properties , DLJ Real Estate Capital Partners and Deutsche Finance Group. The ownership group had been in talks with a buyer to purchase the property for $330M, Bank OZK said in a July earnings statement, but those plans fell through. In its October earnings release , Bank OZK said it had taken control of the property and had to write down its value by $37M. The lab building carried a value of $132M, 80% of its assessed value. Leggat McCall responded to Bisnow 's request for comment by providing a statement from Bank OZK that indicates they are still working together. “808 Windsor is a high-quality asset with excellent long-term potential," Bank OZK Executive Managing Director Cliffton Hill said in the statement. "We have engaged Leggat McCall Properties to work with us on executing a business plan, including leasing, to ensure best-in-class operation and outcomes for the property." A Bank OZK spokesperson confirmed the title transfer, saying the bank has engaged a property manager and is in "ongoing discussions with an interested purchaser." In 2021, Bank OZK provided the development team with a $246M loan to build 808 Windsor. The project was completed in 2024 . In August, the Deutsche Finance Group fund that invested in the property, Deutsche Finance Investment Fund 17 — Club Deal Boston II, said it planned to file for insolvency due to the failure to find a buyer for the property and to get an extension on the loan, Bloomberg reported . The Windsor Street property is part of a larger planned life sciences campus called Boynton Yards . The development team has also completed development of 101 South St., a purpose-built lab building that is 100% leased to Flagship Pioneering . The planned 1.8M SF campus has three other phases that haven't broken ground yet: two lab projects and a 350-unit residential building. In September, the Boynton Yards team filed a zoning text amendment request that would reduce the proposed commercial floor area from 75% to 60%, allowing more residential development on the campus. "Market conditions have since changed considerably, with the life science sector experiencing a sustained downturn in leasing demand and elevated vacancy that has made it increasingly difficult to finance and deliver new lab space and likely will for the foreseeable future," the applicants wrote. "At the same time, there is an acute regional and national housing shortage, and transit-served, underutilized sites like Boynton Yards, located immediately adjacent to the MBTA Green Line's Union Square Station, are ideal locations for additional housing production," the applicant added. The development team was also planning to pursue another life sciences project — a 262K SF property at 15 McGrath Highway in Somerville — but due to the weakening fundamentals in the market, the team put a hold on the project in 2024. The foreclosure comes as the local life sciences market continues to deal with a major oversupply of lab space. The submarket just north of Boston that includes Somerville has been hit particularly hard, with its vacancy rate surpassing 47% at the end of the third quarter, according to CBRE . The building was part of a wave of lab projects that broke ground speculatively during the industry's pandemic-era boom period and then struggled to lease up after demand evaporated. Another one of those projects, a 469K SF building Greystar delivered in Somerville in 2024, landed its first tenant last month, signing a 105K SF lease with Mass General Brigham. items.title: AI borrowers now drive nearly half of long-dated U.S. IG issuance. PIMCO sees 3 diversifiers
items.description: Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Artificial intelligence-related borrowing is becoming a larger share of long-dated U.S. corporate debt — prompting investors to look beyond Big Tech for credit diversification. Investors could consider agency mortgage-backed securities, higher-rated private mortgage bonds and emerging market debt as credit portfolio diversifiers in a corporate debt market increasingly shaped by the AI build-out, according to Lotfi Karoui, managing director and multi-asset strategist at PIMCO. Karoui said AI-related bond issuance now weighs heavily on the broader debt market. Such borrowers now account for almost half of year-to-date gross issuance of non-financial U.S. investment-grade debt with maturities beyond 15 years, PIMCO said in a note Nov. 10. AI hyperscaler debt issuance is projected at around $250 billion in dollar-denominated bonds this year, according to Goldman Sachs forecasts. Estimates for the wider AI ecosystem debt issuance this year — which includes chipmakers, utilities and data center developers — range between $300 billion and $570 billion. There are growing concerns about an AI build-out slowdown prompted by the Democrats' sweeping victory in the U.S. midterm elections, which could pose a headache for long-duration investors looking for diversification, particularly as longer-dated U.S. Treasurys — the traditional duration portfolio hedge — have been rattled by volatility for much of 2026. "For most of the past 3 years, the AI investment boom has been an equity story, but it is increasingly becoming a bond-market story," said Kevin Thozet, a member of Carmignac's investment committee. "The numbers are becoming too large for bonds investors to ignore." Karoui said that within corporate credit, financials offer a large pool of IG exposure with much less direct sensitivity to the AI capex cycle, while "old economy" sectors such as energy can play a similar role in high-yield (HY) markets. "Both, however, are expensive, in our view," Karoui said. "Their spreads above like-maturity Treasuries generally appear tight relative to their risk-adjusted return potential." "Instead, we see other opportunities with more favorable diversification characteristics for investors wary of AI-related investment themes." Agency mortgage-backed securities Mortgage-backed securities backed by U.S. home loans guaranteed by government-sponsored enterprises like Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae have proved more resilient to higher rates and rate volatility this year compared with 2023, Karoui said. The note referenced PIMCO and Bloomberg data highlighting a 33-basis-point pickup in agency MBS over U.S. investment-grade corporate spreads as of Nov. 5, but without the same exposure to corporate borrowers. "In the U.S., high-quality securitized products such as agency mortgage-backed securities and non-agency residential MBS may provide meaningful uncorrelated exposure to the AI theme while still offering decent excess carry versus the broader investment grade market," Karoui said. Higher-rated private mortgage bonds PIMCO also pointed to senior, AAA-rated portions of bonds backed by mortgages that do not qualify for the Qualified Mortgage category under federal ability-to-repay rules. Here, Karoui said that in AAA-rated non-qualified mortgage tranches, the "potential benefits likely outweigh risks." Specifically, the risk stems more from repayments taking longer than expected, rather than the risk that borrowers will fail to pay. That risk has pushed returns higher, while certain newer deals are structured to repay senior investors more quickly and offer protection against losses. "We think the repricing in AAA non-QM creates an intriguing opportunity," Karoui said. "Wider spreads largely compensate investors for extension risk and structural risk tied to materially higher expected credit losses, and today's new issues embed better mitigations against those risks than earlier deals." Emerging market debt Bonds issued by emerging market governments and companies offer another diversification play to U.S. Big Tech. "Although there are pockets of EM with meaningful AI exposure, notably South Korea and Taiwan, much of that is an equity story rather than a fixed income one," said Karoui. "For bond portfolios, EM debt therefore remains a relatively differentiated source of yield, duration, and country-specific risk." He zeroed in on U.S. dollar-denominated emerging market investment-grade "semi-liquid" bond deals — used to finance infrastructure investment — noting they have offered a median pickup of around 40 basis points this year compared to plain vanilla EM bonds. He also flagged opportunities beyond the main benchmarks, including in commodity-exporting countries, while noting that in local-currency bonds, exchange-rate swings can add to returns or erode them. "To be clear, it is not that EM is a lower-risk asset class. Rather, it is that EM debt is exposed to a mix of political, fiscal, and monetary forces that are different than the risks facing the domestic U.S. market," Karoui said. items.title: Why the 2026 fake foreclosure crisis never happened
items.description: The 2026 foreclosure crisis that some people predicted has failed to materialize, and now those people look silly. We should be thankful for the regulations and laws enacted that laid the foundation for such a sound housing credit market: The 2005 bankruptcy reform law and the 2010 Dodd-Frank laws that established qualified mortgage guidelines were historically positive for the U.S. economy. Looking at the New York Fed's Household Debt and Credit Report for Q3, we can clearly see that the anticipated foreclosure crisis hasn't happened. All the headlines showing a high percentage of year-over-year growth in foreclosure data didn’t amount to anything near a crisis. For those who expected a situation worse than what we experienced in 2008, it has been an embarrassing year. This highlights the dangers of listening to economic discussions from those without the necessary expertise. So let’s talk about where these doomers get it wrong. The idea that the FHA foreclosure moratorium, which ended in October 2025, would lead to a surge in distressed listings has been a popular topic this year. It's gotten a lot of headlines, but has fallen flat on its face, since that isn’t how the foreclosure-to-listing process works in America. At minimum, it takes 9-18 months from the start of the foreclosure process to finally add that supply to the marketplace. And foreclosure data has not, at any point since 2014, shown any material sign of credit stress building up in the pipeline. Always remember, 1%-4% of all mortgages are always going to be in delinquency; it’s when that data breaks above historical norms that it should get everyone’s attention. To illustrate what a true foreclosure crisis might look like, we can consider the historical context: since World War II, we have experienced 13 recessions with an average unemployment rate of 7.8%, but only one significant foreclosure crisis, which was the run-up to the 2008 Great Recession. It took four years for the foreclosure credit market to build up before the 2008 recession hit. As we finish Q3 of 2026, we still haven't returned to pre-COVID levels of foreclosure credit stress, as the data below has always shown for anyone who believes in reading. The New York Fed foreclosure credit stress data line moves slowly, and unless this index is above 200, there isn't much activity out of the norm. The many posts this year predicting a foreclosure crisis have proven to be exaggerated. The scale of the situation is small, and it's clear that many commentators lack the experience to accurately discuss the current market conditions. Additionally, I want to highlight HousingWire’s new listing data . During the previous housing crisis, credit foreclosures directly impacted new listing data, pushing weekly listings to between 250,000 and 400,000 — for years. These listings represented distressed sellers who were forced to sell in an underwater market. All those increases from 2005-2008 in foreclosures eventually became distressed sales, and none of that is happening today. Let's compare the new listings data for last week to the same week from 2009-2011: 2009: 280,400 new listings 2010: 353,457 new listings 2011: 352,030 new listings 2026: 54,478 new listings We're missing a credit boom/bust The 2008 massive credit boom and bust took many years to create. We have not seen this kind of credit boom in housing from 2010-2026, so it’s impossible to have a credit bust like 2008 — or "worse than 2008," as many untrained fake housing analysts have talked about for years. A lot of people can’t let go of the past, as they’re still dancing with the ghost of the 2008 housing crisis. They should relax, have a glass of wine, and reflect on their bad takes. In contrast, over the last 16 years, FICO scores in America have remained strong. Most homeowners have 30-year fixed-rate mortgages, and qualification guidelines are much more stringent and effective now. Rising wages and homeowners staying in their properties longer have contributed to the overall financial health of American households. Despite claims of an impending foreclosure crisis, the reality is quite different. In 2010, over 23% of homes in America were underwater, with loan-to-value ratios reaching nearly 86% in 2011. Currently, the loan-to-value figure is down to 44.2%, as the chart below shows. It's crucial to be cautious about who you listen to, as the narrative of a looming crisis has been overstated for many years. If someone tells you it’s housing 2008 or a foreclosure crisis is here, tell them to read a book instead of burning it, and read HousingWire. Related More: Foreclosure

items.title: DC Gym Shooter Kills His Building Manager After HOA Dispute Over Mold Issues
items.description: A Washington, DC, doctor who had been locked in a legal battle with his homeowners’ association over mold problems fatally shot the manager of his condominium as part of a shooting spree on Thursday, according to police. The fatal shooting incident was reported around 8 a.m. in the Logan Circle neighborhood in Northwest DC, about a mile from the White House, drawing dozens of heavily armed police officers to the area. Dr. Matt Wade Lambert , a physician living in a penthouse apartment at the Metropole Condos building on 15th Street Northwest, was publicly identified by the authorities as the shooter who killed one and injured four others before taking his own life. Lambert is suspected of going down to the luxury fitness center VIDA housed inside the building, locating the building manager next to the treadmills, and shooting him from a point blank range, D.C. Councilmember Brooke Pinto told reporters, per WUSA9 . "Within seconds there was a man who fell to the ground, and a pool of blood came out," gym goer James Spellman told the Associated Press . "One gym member rushed to help him. He was instantly dead. He had been shot in the neck." Loading... An armed police officer is seen at the scene of a deadly shooting at Logan Circle in Washington, DC. Dozens of people were in the middle of their morning workout inside the gym at the time of the deadly attack, which triggered an evacuation and a shelter in place order in the area. While law enforcement officials have not revealed an official motive for the shooting, Pinto said that the building manager was "targeted" by the suspect. Lambert then ran out of the gym and shot four other people in the vicinity, among them three construction workers who were across the street. Interim D.C. Police Chief Jeffery Carroll said one of the victims was hospitalized in critical condition and three others sustained non-life-threatening injuries. Loading... The gunman turned the gun on himself inside his penthouse unit while on the phone with police negotiators during the shooting incident in Washington, DC, Thursday. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images Lambert eventually barricaded himself inside his condo at Metropole Circle and was on the phone with police negotiators when he turned the gun on himself, committing suicide. D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser described the incident as a "senseless act of gun violence." Legal feud over mold Court records reviewed by Realtor.com® indicate that Lambert had been in a long-standing feud with his condo’s management and filed a lawsuit in March 2025, alleging that he had not been able to live in his seventh-floor penthouse since Nov. 11, 2024, because of mold, moisture, foul odor, and related damage. Lambert argued in the 12-page complaint that the problems in his unit were caused by repairs to the building’s facade that had been performed by a contractor, for which he paid over $15,000 as part of a special assessment. Loading... The suspect, Dr. Matt Lambert, sued the homeowners' association at Metropole Condo last year over mold and moisture problems. Google Earth According to the filing, Lambert has incurred damages topping $100,000 as a result of the homeowners association's "failure to take corrective action to remedy the moisture accumulation." A mediation in the case had been scheduled for March 2027. items.title: Joanna Gaines Reveals How Her Approach to Holiday Decorating Has Evolved as She’s Gotten Older
items.description: Joanna Gaines keeps a beautifully decorated home year-round, so it’s no surprise that she pulls out all the stops for the holidays . The “Fixer Upper” star recently shared her best holiday hosting tips as she prepares to celebrate the season with her family. She also noted the surprising way her approach has changed over time. “The older I get, the more free I feel to deck the halls,” Gaines, 48, told USA Today . “I do think this is the one time of year where you can really go big if you want to—or keep things timeless and simple.” While the Magnolia co-founder encouraged aspiring decorators to feel empowered to go big with their festive displays, she left room for those who prefer to take a more subdued route. “There’s no right or wrong because the holidays really are so personal and sentimental,” she said. “It’s just a matter of what you love and how you want your home to feel for your family.” Loading... Joanna Gaines is getting ready for the holidays, sharing her best decor tips and getting Magnolia Market ready. Instagram/Joanna Gaines Gaines also noted that she’s committed to upholding food traditions, using recipes she’s been working on since she and Chip Gaines wed in 2003. “Food is really at the center of our holidays,” she said. “Thanksgiving especially is this day I feel like I can taste all year long because our family really does make the same dishes year after year.” Gaines also detailed her approach to Christmas in the editor’s note she published in the Nov. 10 issue of Magnolia Journal . “Every season holds a blend of the big and small, the milestones and the everyday, the photo-worth celebrations and the not-so-picture-perfect moments,” she wrote. “There’s something about the holidays that bridges the gap between these.” She noted that as the years go by, she’s “come to realize” that the most important memories are the ones that might not be captured with a camera, and exist only in memory. “Maybe there’s no physical evidence they happened at all, except for the fact that you were there—and you felt it,” Gaines continued. “It’s these softer moments that give us life and ground us in presence. The days that held no agenda, the mornings I took slow, the smiles you won’t see in my camera roll because I was simply bearing witness.” Loading... “The older I get, the more free I feel to deck the halls,” said the HGTV star, 48. Courtesy of Magnolia Network Loading... Gaines is a big fan of decorating for the holidays and shared a look at her family working together to deck the halls last year. Instagram/Joanna Gaines Explaining that she’s choosing to prioritize holding space for both the major moments and the much more relatable ones, Gaines also reflected on being the “gatekeeper” of her family’s yearly traditions as she aims to “do the same things” they always have, “if not bigger and better” this year. She wrote about the “dressing up” that is encouraged toward the end of the year and romanticized the “fresh delight” of decorating the home, hosting loved ones, and “trying to create standout experiences” that her “kids will remember and tell their kids about someday.” The Gaineses certainly have their hands full with their five children : Drake , 21, Ella , 20, Duke , 18, Emmie , 16, and Crew , 8. But during a recent conversation on the “Not Gonna Lie with Kylie Kelce ” podcast, the proud mom revealed that they’d recently been discussing the idea of expanding the family once again . “When I had Crew at 40, I said, ‘Chip, I want him to have more siblings,” she said. “I really thought I’d have nine children. I’m that lady. Look at my hair. Don’t I look like a lady that would have nine kids? And he was not open to it. Guess who’s open to it now? At 48?” “He is telling everyone I’m pregnant. And just for the record, I’m not,” Gaines quipped, adding that her husband had even told their “grown kids” that she was expecting, and their eldest daughter said that she’s “not coming home” if the news is true. The HGTV personality went on to encourage Kelce, a mom of four, to add another little one to her family. “Five is a good number,” Gaines said, noting that she would “have more babies” if she “could.” Get real estate news in your inbox Sign up now Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

items.title: More Than Half of Raleigh-Area Residents Have Considered Moving Because of Housing Costs, New Survey Finds
items.description:
More Than Half of Raleigh-Area Residents Have Considered
         Moving Because of Housing Costs, New Survey Finds
       New survey finds widespread concern about affordability and support for
         expanding single-family rental housing for Raleigh-area residents
RALEIGH, N.C. – November 12, 2026 – More than half of Raleigh-area residents have considered
moving because of housing costs, including one in three who have considered leaving the state,
according to a new survey. Yet only one in five knew that Congress recently passed federal legislation,
the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, to address affordability concerns.

The survey also found support for expanding access to single-family housing, including newly built
single-family rental homes. Among the key findings:

   ●   Affordability pressures are widespread: 85% of Raleigh-area residents say housing
       affordability is a serious problem, and 55% have considered moving because of housing costs,
       including 33% who have considered moving to another state.
   ●   Essential workers are feeling it: 67% of respondents say it is hard for teachers, nurses, police
       officers and firefighters to afford to live in the communities where they work.
   ●   Residents want housing choices, including access to single-family homes: 63% believe
       people should have access to single-family homes whether they rent or own, compared to those
       who believe they should only be available to people to own.
   ●   More residents support new rental housing than oppose it: 49% support building more new
       single-family rental homes, compared with 33% opposed.
   ●   Renters are feeling affordability pressures: 67% have considered moving because of housing
       costs, and 65% support building more new single-family rental homes.

“Housing affordability challenges are affecting communities across the country, and these results
underscore the need for more housing options. No single housing type will solve today’s housing
shortage. We need more opportunities for homeownership, more rental choices, and a continued focus
on expanding supply so families can find housing that meets their needs,” said Adrianne Todman,
President and CEO of the National Rental Home Council.

The findings come as North Carolina policymakers continue to weigh housing affordability, following
federal action addressing large institutional purchases of existing single-family homes. The 21st Century
ROAD to Housing Act limits large institutional investors from purchasing existing single-family homes
while protecting investments in preserving and building new housing, including build-to-rent homes.

Despite widespread concern about housing affordability, relatively few Raleigh-area residents are aware
of the recent federal action. For instance, only 20% of Raleigh-area residents surveyed knew Congress
had already acted to restrict large investment companies from purchasing existing single-family homes.

Asked what state lawmakers should prioritize now that federal action is in place, residents pointed first to
expanding affordable housing programs (53%), assistance for first-time homebuyers (46%) and lower
 property taxes (46%). Fewer than one in three (30%) chose additional limits on how many homes large
investment companies can own.

“In Raleigh, rising housing costs are making it harder for families to afford a home in the communities
where they live and work,” said Todman. “As North Carolina lawmakers look toward the 2027 session,
there’s an opportunity to keep working families from being priced out as the region grows.”

About the survey

The survey of 600 Raleigh-area residents was conducted via Pollfish in October 2026.

items.title: Renters comfortably affording a house would need a $14,408 raise to buy one (October Rent Report)
items.description: Renters comfortably affording a house would need a $14,408 raise to buy one (October Rent Report) Rental demand is up 22% as buying a single-family home stretches the budget far further than renting one. Written by Kara Ng on November 12, 2026 A household that can comfortably afford to rent a single-family home would need a $14,408 annual raise to afford the monthly costs of owning a home. Rental demand is up 22.1% year over year nationwide, as measured by the Zillow Observed Renter Demand Index, with demand for single-family rentals up 24.3%. The typical U.S. single-family rent was $2,243 a month in October, up 3.2% from a year ago, while the typical multifamily rent was $1,744, up 2.5%, according to the Zillow Observed Rent Index. Wanting a more suburban lifestyle — the extra space, yard and private garage that often come with a single-family home — doesn’t always mean stretching the budget to buy. In fact, it’s a stretch most families aren’t prepared to make, especially when a household comfortably affording the rent for a single-family home would need a $14,408 pay raise to cover the monthly costs of owning one, even before saving for a down payment. Nationally, the typical single-family rent is $2,243 a month, compared with $2,603 a month to own a single-family home with 20% down, or $360 more each month. To comfortably afford those costs — the rule of thumb being to spend no more than 30% of its income on housing — a household needs an income of $89,724 to rent and $104,132 to buy. For many households, renting a house is a choice and not a fallback. It takes less income than owning, and it leaves more room in the monthly budget. The size of the raise depends on the market The pay raise needed to buy is now the highest since early 2025, more than double the $6,463 it took in February 2026, when mortgage rates briefly fell below 6%. The gap looks very different from market to market. It’s largest in San Jose, where the income needed to buy ($404,925) is more than double the income needed to rent ($190,561), a gap of $214,364. The next largest gap is in San Francisco ($139,353), followed by San Diego ($84,101), New York ($78,208) and Los Angeles ($78,003). The smallest annual gaps are in Pittsburgh ($2,554), Houston ($4,500) and Cincinnati ($4,774). Buffalo is the only market where buying would not require a raise. Even with such a raise, would-be buyers still face another hurdle: saving a 20% down payment. About 30% of mortgage buyers use a gift or loan from family or friends, and 46% draw on two or more sources, including the use of down payment assistance programs , according to Zillow’s 2026 Consumer Housing Trends Report . In addition to the monthly cost, households deciding between renting and buying should weigh the upfront costs of buying, the chance to build equity and the opportunity for renters to invest their down payment instead. Zillow’s rent vs. buy research puts the national break-even timeline — the number of years a household would need to own before buying comes out ahead — at 7.8 years with 20% down. Rental demand keeps climbing As renting a house becomes an increasingly better value, more shoppers are turning to rentals. Rental demand is up 22.1% year over year nationwide, according to the Zillow Observed Renter Demand Index (ZORDI). Demand for single-family rentals is up 24.3%, roughly double the 12.1% rise for multifamily rentals. Rental demand surges in the Bay Area and the Sun Belt Demand rose the most in San Jose, where ZORDI is up 78.9% from a year ago, followed by San Francisco (60.5%), Austin (59.6%), Miami (51.5%) and Jacksonville (47.9%). San Jose and San Francisco are also among the markets where buying is furthest out of reach, and where rents are rising quickly, up 8.9% and 12.2% respectively. In Austin, Miami and Jacksonville, rent growth is more moderate, at 1.1%, 2.1% and 2.6%. Not every market is following the national trend. ZORDI is down year over year in Providence (-4.3%), Richmond (-1.9%), Baltimore (-1.7%), Hartford (-1.3%) and Washington, D.C. (-0.9%). items.description: Existing-Home Sales Decreased 5.5% in October, According to NAR Report Section Menu NAR Media Contacts Statistical Release Schedule Op-Eds & Letters to the Editor NAR Fact Sheet NAR in the News More November 12, 2026 Media Contact: Media Relations Mortgages & Home Financing , Financing & Credit , Residential Real Estate Share View and share infographic Month-Over-Month Existing-home sales decreased 5.5% to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million in October. Unsold inventory increased 1.3% to 1.59 million units, equal to a 5.1-month supply. Year-Over-Year Existing-home sales decreased 8.8%. The median existing-home sales price increased 0.4% to $416,700. WASHINGTON (November 12, 2026) – Existing-home sales decreased by 5.5% month-over-month and decreased by 8.8% year-over-year, according to the National Association of REALTORS® Existing-Home Sales report. The report provides the real estate ecosystem, including agents, homebuyers and sellers, with data on the level of home sales, price and inventory. Month-over-month sales declined in the Midwest, South and West and held steady in the Northeast. Year-over-year sales declined in all four regions. “Home buying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023. As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010,” said NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun. “Despite fewer transactions in October, the 88 million homeowners across the country are largely in a comfortable financial position due to sizable housing wealth accumulation. The number of distressed property sales remains historically low at only 2% of all transactions,” Yun said. “Based on the current underwhelming home sales pace at a time of consistent job growth, there could be sizable pent-up demand if mortgage rates decline.” National Snapshot Total Existing-Home Sales for October Existing-home sales decreased 5.5% month-over-month. 1 Existing-home sales decreased 8.8% year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million. Inventory in October Total housing inventory was 1.59 million units, up 1.3% from September and 4.6% from October 2025. 2 Unsold inventory represented a 5.1-month supply, up from 4.7 months in September and 4.4 months in October 2025. Median Sales Price in October The median existing-home price for all housing types was $416,700. 3 The median price increased 0.4% from $414,900 one year ago, marking the 40th consecutive month of year-over-year price increases. Housing Affordability in October The Housing Affordability Index registered at 100.7, down from 107.3 one year ago. Year-over-year, affordability declined in all four regions. The median home price was $421,900, up 0.4% from one year ago. Condominiums and Co-ops in October Sales decreased 2.9% month-over-month to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 340,000. Sales were down 10.5% from one year ago. The median price was $365,100, up 0.3% from October 2025. The median price was $624,300, unchanged from October 2025. REALTORS® Confidence Index for October The median time on market was 35 days, up from 33 days in September and 34 days in October 2025. Individual investors and second-home buyers accounted for 20% of transactions, unchanged from September and up from 16% in October 2025. Learn more in our FAQs . The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.11% as of November 12, 2026, down from last week when it averaged 7.18%. A year ago at this time, the 30-year FRM averaged 6.24%. The 15-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 6.45%, down from last week when it averaged 6.57%. A year ago at this time, the 15-year FRM averaged 5.49%. PMMS results are released weekly on Thursdays at 12 p.m. ET. and are an average of loan rates offered the prior Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Compare Historical PMMS Results Frequently Asked Questions Toggle all accordion sections Expand All What data is used for PMMS? The PMMS results are based on data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA): mortgage rates collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . How is the national average determined? We collect the mortgage rate of all purchase applications based on PMMS criteria and a national average mortgage rate is calculated out of all the selected loan applications. The criteria include weekly conventional, single-family originations with conforming loan limits as set by FHFA. Is the PMMS rate based on current lender quotes or recent settlements? PMMS rates are based on applications submitted to Freddie Mac for the given week from lenders across the country. What type of lenders are included in the PMMS? Currently, our lenders are a mix of credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies. Do the PMMS results represent the rates charged on a specific day of the week? If so, which day? Or are they the average rate charged that week? PMMS is published each Thursday at noon ET. When a U.S. holiday falls on a Thursday, the PMMS will publish on the Wednesday of that week. The week of application activity starts at 12:00 a.m. ET the prior Thursday and lasts through 11:59 p.m. ET Wednesday. Therefore, the PMMS results are an average of loan rates offered Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Why are adjustable rates no longer published? ARMs indexed to alternatives to U.S. Treasury securities have become more prevalent in the market. As we worked on enhancing the PMMS , we carefully considered which loan products were most popular for the PMMS borrower profile (good/excellent credit, 20% loans, home purchase loans on owner occupied 1-unit single-family properties). Additionally, in recent years the mortgage market has been dominated by fixed mortgage products. While there has been an uptick recently in the share of adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) for the broader mortgage market, ARMs remain most popular for higher loan size (nonconforming) loans. Why are fees/points no longer published? Under the current LPA requirements, fees and points are not always required to be provided by lenders. Therefore, we are not able to report on the average fees and points. How has PMMS changed over time? Since April 1971, Freddie Mac shared the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate with the PMMS. We have updated the information we collect and the process for gathering data over time. Changes in Data Processes When it was launched, PMMS surveyed lenders on the rates and points for their most popular 30-year fixed-rate, 15-year fixed-rate and 5/1 hybrid amortizing adjustable-rate mortgage products. The survey was based on first-lien prime conventional conforming home purchase mortgages with a loan-to-value of 80 percent. In addition, the adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) products were indexed to U.S. Treasury yields, and lenders were asked for both the initial coupon rate and points as well as the margin on the ARM products. Lenders surveyed each week were a mix of lender types — credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies — roughly proportional to the level of mortgage business that each type commands nationwide. On November 17, 2022, the mortgage rate gathering process was updated. Instead of surveying lenders, we now use data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA). Changes in Information Shared In 1984 , the 1-year ARM was added to the survey. In 1991 , the 15-year fixed-rate mortgage rate was added. In January 2005 , a 5/1 hybrid ARM series was added. In January 2016 , the 1-year ARM was discontinued. In November 2022 , adjustable rates and fees/points were discontinued. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . items.description: Cushman & Wakefield Named Top Ten Military Friendly® Employer for Fifth Consecutive Year, Expands Veteran Career Pathways Nationwide Phoebe Schmidt • 11/11/2026 Veteran's Day 2026 New York -- Cushman & Wakefield (NYSE: CWK) announced today that the real estate services firm has been recognized as a Top Ten Military Friendly® Employer for the fifth consecutive year. As the nation celebrates America's 250th anniversary, the firm continues expanding opportunities for veterans transitioning to civilian careers, with a particular focus on skilled trades and technical professions. "As the United States marks its 250th anniversary, we're reminded that the country's strength has always depended on people willing to serve something larger than themselves," said Bruce Mosler , Chairman of Global Brokerage. "Veterans leave the military with experience leading teams, solving problems under pressure and taking responsibility when the stakes are high. Those qualities are increasingly difficult to find and impossible to teach overnight. Creating opportunities for veterans isn't simply a way to honor their service. It's an investment in the future workforce and leadership of this country." Cushman & Wakefield employs more than 1,400 veterans across its U.S. operations and has plans to hire an additional 500 veterans this year. Through its Military & Veterans Programs, the firm provides recruitment, mentorship and career-transition support, including participation in the Department of War's SkillBridge program and military spouse employment initiatives. The firm's approach to veteran hiring and engagement has also been shared with more than 300 companies nationwide as a model for building effective post-military career pathways. The opportunity is significant. U.S. employers reported approximately 325,000 job openings in construction and 608,000 in manufacturing in July 2026, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. More than 160,000 people leave military service annually with experience maintaining aircraft, vehicles, facilities, electrical systems and heavy equipment. These capabilities can translate directly to civilian careers, including building engineering, HVAC, facilities operations and project management. To help veterans and military spouses explore careers in the skilled trades, Cushman & Wakefield partnered with 50strong in September to launch the Skilled Trades Mentor Hub. The initiative connects transitioning service members, veterans and military spouses with professionals who can help them understand career options and how their experience translates to civilian roles. "Much of the conversation today is focused on AI, automation and how technology is reshaping the workforce," added Matt Disher , Executive Director, Military & Veterans Programs. "What often gets overlooked is that service members have been operating sophisticated technologies, complex systems and mission-critical equipment for years. They understand how to adapt when technology changes because they've been doing it throughout their military careers. As employers look for talent that can learn quickly, solve problems and operate in high-consequence environments, veterans are exceptionally well positioned to help lead that transformation across industries." In addition to being named a Top Ten Military Friendly® Employer for the fifth consecutive year, the firm was recently recognized as one of America's Most Patriotic Companies 2026 by Newsweek for its support of veterans, service members and military-connected communities. Institutions earning the Military Friendly® Employers designation are evaluated using both public data sources and responses from a proprietary survey. Over 1,200 companies participated in the 2026 survey. "Earning the Military Friendly® designation is more than a badge; it's a reflection of deep-rooted values and strategic foresight," said Kayla Lopez, Vice President of Memberships, Military Friendly®. "These organizations don't just open doors for veterans, spouses, and service members; they build pathways for lasting impact. Their commitment isn't performative; it's transformative. It's proof that honoring military talent is not only the right thing to do, it's the smart thing to do." Cushman & Wakefield will be featured in the 2027 Military Friendly® Employers list published in the Winter issue of G.I. Jobs® magazine and online at www.militaryfriendly.com. In 2025, the firm reported revenue of $10.3 billion across its core service lines of Services, Leasing, Capital markets, and Valuation and other. items.description: HighlightsOperating conditions in the Denver multifamily market remained stable during the third quarter, with vacancy holding steady and rents increasing for a third consecutive quarter.
