items.title: VA default remains low despite record debt
items.description: Low default rates obscure record debt exposure across the expanding VA mortgage market. VA loans drive 9.5% of purchase originations, with average balances tripling to $418,000. Serious delinquency is low at 2.0% (vs. 5.0% for FHA), but record loan sizes amplify dollar risk. Zero-down financing and no monthly mortgage insurance make VA loans a vital hedge against high rates. Veterans are borrowing more money than ever before, and by conventional benchmarks, the VA loans asset class looks remarkably disciplined. According to Cotality data, delinquencies are sitting at a 2.0% — down from a year ago and roughly a third of the 6.5% pandemic peak, and well below the 5.0% recorded across the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) book. But a reassuring percentage can obscure an expensive reality. Low rates, record exposure The volume of distressed veteran mortgage debt is substantially larger than at any point in the last 20 years. In 2005, VA purchase loans were a niche product accounting for just 1.4% of purchase originations. Now they account for nearly ten times that number. VA purchase originations: Count and amount Data source: Cotality, 2026 One in every ten closed loans are VA-funded, which is actually down from their peak popularity in 2021 when VA originations surged near 282,000 loans, generating roughly $100 billion in volume across 2021 and 2022. But alongside the number of loans increasing, the average VA purchase balance has more than tripled, climbing from $122,500 in 1998 to $418,000 in 2026. When the pandemic-era competition recalibrated price ceilings, loan balances accelerated sharply from $286,000 to $355,000 in just two years. That popularity has mathematical consequences. A 2% delinquency on a portfolio of $122,500 loans comprising 1.4% of originations could be written off as an operational blip. But 2% delinquency on a $418,000 baseline across nearly a tenth of the national purchase market translates to billions in non-performing principal. Average VA purchase share by loan count Data source: Cotality, 2026 That risk isn’t due to borrowers failing at a higher rate. The size of VA loan portfolios has simply expanded to the point where small percentage slippages represent significant dollar exposure. Webinar Veteran Homeownership: Turning Service into Generational Wealth Affording stability This dramatic expansion in loan balances was not born of speculation, but of survival in a housing market where affordability is strained. With mortgage rates and home prices at near generational highs, the conventional path to homeownership is bending out of reach for millions . Accumulating a traditional 10% to 20% down payment on the national median home price of $429,450 demands $42,000 to $84,000 in liquid savings—a barrier that sidelines even buyers with comfortable earnings. Average VA purchase loan amount Data source: Cotality, 2026 ‍ A VA loan offers an achievable alternative. By offering loans with little to no downpayment requirement and eliminating monthly mortgage insurance requirements, this Ginnie Mae-backed option allows eligible service members and veterans to enter the market without draining cash reserves. When income shocks arrive, that liquidity buffer can keep families in their homes. That structural safety net is why VA loans crested at only 6.5% serious delinquency during the 2020 market tumult, while FHA loans spiked to 12.2% *. The defense corridors Because military demographics are highly geographic, this heavy-balance exposure is not even across the country, with clusters appearing in specific regional economies: Alaska: VA financing drives 28% of the funds put towards all home purchase originations. Virginia: VA loans account for 22% of the total dollar amount of all originations. Hawaii: VA transactions 20% of the total dollars that people put toward buying a home ‍ VA purchase dollar amount by state Data source: Cotality, 2026 In these markets, the VA loan is the bedrock of local housing turnover. Any shift in federal loan limits, interest rate trajectories, or military deployment cycles triggers an outsized local shock. The VA loan has become a high-balance, high-volume credit engine. For mortgage originators and servicers, the payment discipline of this population offers security, but the larger loan sizes mean there is far less margin for error when local job markets or regional housing valuations stumble. For servicers and secondary-market investors managing these pools, the priority is no longer just tracking the headline delinquency rate. It is managing the sheer weight of the capital behind it. items.description: ATTOM Reveals July as Best Month to Buy a Home Based on Lowest Premium above AVM by ATTOM Team | Nov 12, 2026 | Home Sales & Prices , Real Estate News - Recent Articles July and November Offer Lowest Homebuying Premiums; December 24th Is the Lowest Single Day IRVINE, Calif. — Nov. 12, 2026 — ATTOM , the leading provider of property data , AI-powered intelligence , and real estate analytics solutions, today released its annual analysis highlighting the best days and months of the year to purchase a home. The report found that July offers the lowest premium of any month at 6.3 percent above market value, followed by November at 7.4 percent. Additionally, December 24 stands out as the single best day to buy a home. According to ATTOM’s latest analysis of more than 48 million single-family home and condo sales over the past 10 years, buyers who close on December 24 are seeing the lowest premium above the automated valuation model (AVM). While still above market value, homebuyers are only paying a 3.2 percent premium, compared to the 14.5 percent premium buyers are seeing on May 27, the highest of any day that occurs every year. (Full methodology is enclosed below.) Other days of the year offering lower premiums for homebuyers include: July 10 (3.5 percent premium above market value); July 9 (4.1 percent premium); July 3 (4.3 percent premium); July 2 (4.3 percent premium); and July 17 (4.6 percent premium). In total, nine of the ten lowest-premium days of the year fall in July. ATTOM’s latest analysis also looked at the best months to buy at the national level and best months to buy at the state level. Best Months to Buy Nationally, the best months to buy are July (6.3 percent premium above market value); November (7.4 percent premium); October (7.8 percent premium); September (8.2 percent premium); and December (8.2 percent premium). Best Months to Buy by State According to the study, Hawaii (-1.8 percent in January) and Michigan (-1.7 percent in November) are the only states where buyers saw a discount below full market value in their best month. Buyers in three other states paid close to market value at their best time of year: Connecticut (0.0 percent in January); Minnesota (0.0 percent in December); and Illinois (0.1 percent premium in November). Powering Real Estate Businesses with Property Data and Analytics Solutions For Every Industry Methodology For this analysis ATTOM looked at any calendar day in the last 10 years (2016 to 2025) with at least 10,000 single family home and condo sales. There were 362 days (including leap year data) that matched these criteria, with the four exceptions being Jan. 1, July 4, Nov. 11, and Dec. 25. To calculate the premium or discount paid on a given day, ATTOM compared the median sales price for homes with a purchase closing on that day with the median automated valuation model (AVM) for those same homes at the time of sale. The premium is the percentage by which the median sales price exceeds the median AVM. A negative figure is a discount.
